title: Forgiving yourself
hookLine: the sources that speak of being forgiven also leave room to forgive yourself

cards: The meeting was three weeks ago. Dana said the sharp thing, the room went quiet, and she apologized first thing the next morning. Her coworker waved it off: honestly, it's fine, already forgotten.

And still, in the shower, at a red light, at two in the morning, the scene plays again, with Dana cast as the villain. She has forgiven people for much worse. The one she can't seem to reach is herself.
The old texts have a few things to say about that last person in line. Today: forgiving yourself.

teach.h: AS FAR AS THE EAST IS FROM THE WEST.
teach.b: First, the Psalms. Psalm 103 says how far forgiveness carries a wrong away: "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet.
In the psalm, a forgiven wrong isn't kept on a shelf, to be taken down again at two in the morning.

teach.h: THE MOON IS NOT THE CLOUDS.
teach.b: Second, the Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, in Max Müller's translation: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds."
It doesn't say the deeds never happened. The clouds were real. But the moon is not the clouds.
Buddhist tradition connects this verse with Angulimala, a man remembered for terrible violence who became a monk. Third, where you stand in the circle.
The Visuddhimagga, a classic Buddhist manual, teaches loving-kindness by starting with yourself: wish yourself well first, as the example, then widen the same wish to others.
You know from the inside how much you want to be happy, so you can wish it for everyone else. When kindness goes around the room: me too. Fourth, this isn't pretending.
The psalm still says transgressions; the verse still says evil deeds.

teach.h: KEEP THE LESSON, DROP THE PUNISHMENT.
teach.b: In this lesson, forgiving yourself comes after the owning: after the apology, after repairing what you can.
What's left is the replay that no longer teaches you anything. Keep the lesson, put down the punishment.

how: In Buddhist loving-kindness practice as the Visuddhimagga describes it, the meditator first wishes themselves well and then extends the wish to others; Jewish and Christian readers often turn to Psalm 103 when speaking about being forgiven.

o: waiting until everyone you hurt has fully forgiven you
owning a wrong, then offering yourself the kindness you give others
deciding the thing you did wasn't really wrong after all

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: the Dhammapada verse says the evil deeds never happened
the clouds were real; the verse says the deeds are covered by good deeds, and the moon comes out.
in the Visuddhimagga, loving-kindness begins with wishing yourself well
you start with yourself as the example, then widen the wish to others.
in today's lesson, forgiving yourself means skipping the apology
it comes after owning the wrong and repairing what you can. the psalm and the verse both still name the wrong.

games.q: you said something sharp, apologized, and the other person says it's already forgotten. the scene keeps replaying for you. what do today's sources point toward?
o: replay it until it stops hurting.
keep the lesson, put down the punishment.
decide it was never your fault.
games.why: the psalm and the Dhammapada both still name the wrong. what they let go of is carrying it forever.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you did that still replays, a sharp word or a promise you let slide, and look at it plainly: yes, that happened, and if something's left to repair, note it for later.

Then place yourself inside the kindness you'd offer a friend who told you this story, and say the Visuddhimagga's simple wish quietly: may I be happy. If you pray, you can bring this to God in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving yourself. Owning what you did, then letting yourself into the same circle of kindness you offer others. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition: loving-kindness, which the Visuddhimagga begins with yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: me too. You belong inside your own kindness as much as anyone. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.
